analysis.body:
The Census Bureau's Business Trends and Outlook Survey recorded 12.6% of utilities firms reporting AI use in the most recent period, down from 17.1% in the prior period, suggesting that measured adoption in this sector is uneven rather than uniformly advancing. The survey covers utilities under NAICS 22, with oil and gas extraction reported separately under mining, so the headline figure captures only part of what the broader energy industry is doing with AI.

The applications being deployed span two distinct parts of the sector. On the grid and generation side, the Electric Power Research Institute runs working groups on AI for grid resilience, wildfire-risk prediction, and asset-health monitoring, functioning as the sector's shared research layer. The Department of Energy's Grid Modernization Initiative carries the federal record of AI projects in real-time grid balancing, reactor optimization, and carbon capture across US utilities, while NextEra Energy, described as the largest US renewable producer, uses AI to forecast wind and solar yield, optimize battery dispatch, and automate plant maintenance. In the subsurface, Baker Hughes deploys AI for autonomous drilling, reservoir simulation, and pipeline monitoring, and Geoteric offers deep-learning interpretation of 3D seismic data, automatically mapping faults for oil, gas, and geothermal exploration, with the company describing this as achieving an unprecedented visualization of the subsurface faster than previously possible.

A specialist vendor layer sits between the large operators and the raw technology. Amperon, founded in 2018 by a former energy trader and data engineer, sells AI and machine learning demand forecasting to utilities, traders, and asset operators, claiming accuracy up to 3x better than existing solutions and regularly beating independent system operators. The company processes about 25 different weather variables every hour across 40,000 weather points from four vendors, blending outputs from three weather sources through an ensemble model. Siemens Energy supplies AI controllers and digital-twin software for gas, wind, and grid assets, representing the pathway by which AI reaches many operators as embedded equipment rather than a separate procurement.

The Department of Energy has quantified the power demand that AI itself creates, which makes energy simultaneously a user and a binding constraint. Per DOE's reporting, data centers consumed about 4.4% of US electricity in 2023, with projections reaching 6.7 to 12% by 2028, driven primarily by AI workloads. DOE has responded by launching a Speed to Power Initiative to accelerate large-scale grid infrastructure development and announcing plans to partner with private-sector developers on AI data centers and energy generation projects on DOE lands. The Department has also released a PermitAI tool to accelerate federal environmental permitting for new generation projects.

On standards and risk, the IEEE Power and Energy Society publishes the technical standards and research covering machine learning in power systems, grid cyber-defense, and distributed energy resource management, providing the engineering baseline that procurement decisions should reference. DOE acknowledges directly that AI systems may generate incorrect, unverifiable, and potentially harmful outputs, and that any deployment must properly understand and mitigate those risks, a posture that reflects the stakes of errors in grid control or safety-critical subsurface decisions. The DOE's Genesis Mission, combining the national laboratories' computing, scientific datasets, and AI capabilities into an integrated system, represents the federal government's long-term strategic bet on AI for energy independence and national security.

A reader evaluating deployment in this sector should note that the measured adoption rate is modest and has moved downward in the Census data, yet the operational evidence from companies like NextEra, Baker Hughes, and Amperon shows substantive use in specific, quantifiable tasks where accuracy improvements are the primary value proposition. The sector's dual position, as both an AI consumer and the physical infrastructure AI depends on, means that grid and forecasting investments are increasingly intertwined with the broader AI buildout, and federal programs through DOE and the Grid Modernization Initiative represent both a funding source and a coordination mechanism for utilities willing to engage them.
